title: How Long Does It Take to Get a Liquor License?
summary: Most liquor licenses take one to three months once your application is complete, but the full process can take six months or more. See timelines by state.
body_markdown:
Most state alcohol agencies process a complete liquor license application in one to three months. The full process usually takes longer. Once you add finding a location that qualifies, getting local approval, and setting up your business, three to six months is a more realistic window. In states with license quotas or a backlog at the state agency, it can stretch past that.


The wait matters because rent, staff, and inventory plans all depend on your opening date, and you can't legally sell a bottle until your license is in hand. This guide breaks down typical timelines in eight states, where the time actually goes, what causes delays, and how to plan your opening around the wait.


## How Long Does a Liquor License Take in Each State?


Alcohol is licensed state by state, so there's no national timeline. Here's what the state agencies themselves say about processing times for retail licenses:


State Typical processing time What affects it


[California](https://www.abc.ca.gov/licensing/frequently-asked-questions/) Most investigations take 55 to 65 days, and a license can't be issued in fewer than 30 Off-sale general licenses are capped at one per 2,500 residents. If a public convenience or necessity finding is needed, the city or county has up to 90 days to decide


[Texas](https://www.tabc.texas.gov/services/tabc-licenses-permits/new-tabc-licenses-permits/) 30-35 days, per TABC. No population quota, but the city or county has to certify the location first


[New York](https://sla.ny.gov/get-license) About 22 to 26 weeks for most applications Most retail businesses can open on a temporary permit in under 30 days, but[new liquor and wine stores don't qualify](https://sla.ny.gov/system/files/documents/2026/01/adivisory_2026-1_-_temporary_permits_for_retail_manufacturing_wholesale_importing_and_brand_owner.pdf) . Transfers of an existing store do


[Florida](https://m.flsenate.gov/Statutes/120.60) Must be processed within 90 days of a complete application Liquor licenses are capped at one per 7,500 residents per county. A temporary license is available


[Washington](https://lcb.wa.gov/licensing/applicant-faqs) 60 to 90 days for retail licenses Objections and requests for more documents add time


[Connecticut](https://portal.ct.gov/dcp/knowledge-base/articles/liquor-control/2026/applications-and-licensing/off-premises-permit/off-premises-application-process) About 3 weeks to a provisional permit and 3 months to a final permit The required placard and newspaper notice takes about two months


[Massachusetts](https://www.mass.gov/how-to/apply-for-an-alcoholic-beverages-retail-license-new-or-transfer) The town must decide within 30 days of filing, then the state ABCC investigates The town must issue the license within 7 days of ABCC approval


[New Jersey](https://nj.gov/oag/abc/downloads/License-Types.pdf) Set by the town, not the state. Package store licenses are issued by the municipality, so timing depends on the local board’s schedule. New package store licenses are capped at one per 7,500 residents per town ([N.J.S.A. 33:1-12.14](https://law.justia.com/codes/new-jersey/title-33/section-33-1-12-14/) ), so most owners buy an existing one


[Indiana](https://www.in.gov/atc/alcohol-permit-resources/alcohol-permit-information/obtaining-an-alcoholic-beverage-permit) New permits can take 10 to 12 weeks A local board hearing comes first. Package store permits are capped by population, so many owners buy one or bid at a state auction


[Ohio](https://com.ohio.gov/divisions-and-programs/liquor-control/new-permit-info/guides-and-resources/licensing-process) No set timeline. Processing starts at least 3 weeks after you apply, and local officials then have 30 to 60 days to object Carryout beer and wine permits are subject to quota. Spirits are sold only through state contract liquor agencies


[Michigan](https://www.michigan.gov/lara/bureau-list/lcc/faq/retailer-faq/licensing-timeline) No set timeline; applications are reviewed in the order received A conditional license is available for new beer-and-wine stores, but not for new spirits licenses


[Georgia](https://dor.georgia.gov/centralized-alcohol-licensing-faqs) No set timeline; the local license must be issued first Once you hold the local license, a temporary permit lets new spirits retailers open for up to 120 days while the state investigates


[Colorado](https://bouldercolorado.gov/services/liquor-licenses) Generally 3-4 months. New liquor stores can't open within 1,500 feet of another off-premises retailer, or 3,000 feet in some small towns


[Idaho](https://isp.idaho.gov/abc/faq/) Up to 90 days by law Private stores sell beer and wine only. Spirits are sold through the state


In Massachusetts and Illinois, the city or town licenses your store first, and in New Jersey the town issues the license itself, so local approval sets much of the timeline.


Texas sits at the other end: there's no quota, and[getting a liquor license in Texas](https://www.santehq.com/blog/blog-how-to-get-texas-liquor-license) is mostly a matter of clearing local certification and filing a complete application. Backlogs change from year to year, so check your state agency's website for current processing times before you set an opening date.


## What Are the Steps to Get a Liquor License, and How Long Does It Take?


The state's review is only one part of the wait. Most of the time goes into the steps before and around it.


### 1. Choose your license and check the location (1 to 4 weeks)


Start by deciding what you'll sell. A full liquor license covers spirits, but if you only plan to stock beer and wine, the[license you need to sell beer](https://www.santehq.com/blog/blog-do-you-need-a-liquor-license-to-sell-beer) is often cheaper and easier to get. Then confirm that the address allows alcohol sales, that it meets any distance rules near schools or churches, and that zoning permits a liquor store.


Do this before you sign a lease. An address that fails any of these checks can't be fixed with better paperwork, and finding out after you've committed to the space is the most expensive mistake in the whole process.


### 2. Get local approval (a few weeks to several months)


This is often the slowest step, and it varies the most. Depending on the state, you may need a zoning sign-off, a conditional use permit with a public hearing, or a full local license before the state will look at your application.


Start by calling your city or county planning department and the town clerk. Ask what approvals a liquor store needs at your address, how often the relevant board meets, and whether a public hearing is required. If your council only meets once a month, missing one filing deadline can push you back four weeks.


### 3. Set up your business (1 to 3 weeks)


Form your LLC or corporation, get an EIN, and register for a sales tax permit. You'll also register with the federal Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau using Form 5630.5d. It's free, and there's no waiting period.


Settle your ownership structure now, because the state will want details on every owner. Adding or changing an owner after you've applied can mean amending the application or starting over.


### 4. Gather your documents (1 to 3 weeks)


Expect to provide personal details for every owner, proof of where your funding comes from, your lease, and a floor plan. Missing or inconsistent paperwork is the most common reason applications get sent back.


Funding documentation deserves extra care. Agencies want to trace every dollar going into the business, so have bank statements, loan documents, or gift letters ready to show where the money came from.


### 5. Pay your fees and file any required bond (1 to 2 weeks)


Most states collect the application fee and the first license fee when you file. Some also require a bond. Texas, for example, requires package stores to file a conduct surety bond of $5,000, or $10,000 if the store is within 1,000 feet of a public school.


### 6. State review and background checks (1 to 6 months)


The state investigates the owners, the funding, and the location. This is the stage the processing times in the table above measure.


During the review, an investigator may ask for missing documents or clarifications. How quickly you respond has a direct effect on how long this stage takes, so check your email and the state's online portal regularly.


### 7. Public notice and objections (where required)


Many states require you to post a notice at the store or publish one in a local newspaper so neighbors and officials can object. California requires a[30-day posting](https://www.abc.ca.gov/information-regarding-alcoholic-beverage-license-applications-and-protests/) at the premises, and Connecticut's placard and newspaper notice takes about two months.


This usually runs alongside the state's review rather than after it. A protest can lead to a hearing and add months, so it helps to introduce yourself to neighbors and local officials early, especially if your location is near homes or schools.


### 8. Complete any required training (a few days)


Some states require new owners or managers to complete alcohol law training before the license is issued. Connecticut, for example, requires new applicants to finish its Liquor Law Education Program. Even where it's optional, training your staff on ID checks before you open protects the license you're about to receive.


### 9. Pass inspection and receive your license


Some states inspect the premises before issuing the license, and agents can keep inspecting after you open. Having your records and layout ready makes this go faster, and a[liquor store inspection checklist](https://www.santehq.com/blog/liquor-store-inspection-checklist) is useful long after your first visit.


Once the license is issued, post it where customers can see it. Your distributors will also need your license details before they can sell to you, so have them ready to send the day it arrives.


## Why Liquor License Timelines Vary So Much


Two owners in the same state can wait very different amounts of time. These are the factors that make the biggest difference:


- **License type:** Beer-and-wine licenses usually move faster than full spirits licenses, and they're less likely to be capped.
- **Quota rules:** In states that cap licenses by population, new ones may only become available through an annual drawing, or not at all. When your county has no licenses left, it's a supply problem rather than a processing delay, and no amount of good paperwork will speed it up. Your real options are the next drawing or buying an existing license.
- **Control states:** In[ABC states](https://www.santehq.com/blog/abc-states-guide-liquor-store-owners) , the state controls some or all spirits sales, so you may be applying for a beer-and-wine license or a state agency contract rather than a standard retail license.
- **New license or transfer:** A transfer skips some steps but adds others, like escrow and a review of the seller's record.
- **Location:** Stores near schools, churches, or homes draw more scrutiny and more chances of a protest.
- **Local government:** Some cities approve applications at a monthly council meeting, while others need a full public hearing.
- **State backlog:** Processing times rise and fall with staffing and demand.


## Is It Faster to Buy an Existing Liquor License?


Sometimes. In quota states, buying a license from a current owner can be the only practical way to get one, since new licenses are released rarely or not at all. California, Florida, and New Jersey all cap licenses by population, and[liquor license costs](https://www.santehq.com/blog/how-much-does-a-liquor-license-cost) on the private market there can run far above the state fee.


Buying doesn't skip the state, though. The agency still has to approve the transfer and check your background and funding, and the money usually sits in escrow until it does. In New Jersey, for example, a transfer requires a newspaper notice published twice, a week apart, and a resolution from the town before the state signs off.


In some states, buying isn't an option at all. Texas permits can't be transferred, so a new owner applies for their own permit even when buying an existing store. In states without quotas, applying for a new license is usually simpler.


## Can You Sell Alcohol While Your Application Is Pending?


Only if your state offers a temporary permit and you qualify for one. A few examples:


- **Florida:** Once you file a complete application with no apparent reason for denial, you can buy a temporary license and start selling right away.
- **Connecticut:** A provisional permit can be approved about three weeks after a complete application, before the final permit is issued.
- **New York:** Temporary permits last 180 days, but new liquor stores and wine stores don't qualify. Transfers of an existing store can.
- **California:** Temporary permits cover some transfers of an existing licensed store but not brand-new licenses, so buying an existing store is often the quickest way to open with a[California off-sale liquor license](https://www.santehq.com/blog/blog-california-liquor-license-for-liquor-stores) .
- **Georgia:** New spirits retailers can get a temporary permit that lets them operate for 120 days while the state's background investigation continues. It's usually issued within two to five business days of the agent's preliminary review.
- **Michigan:** A conditional license lets you operate for up to a year while your application is finalized. It's available for new beer-and-wine stores and some ownership transfers, but not for new spirits licenses.
- **Colorado:** The local licensing authority may issue a temporary permit while a transfer of ownership is pending.
- **Idaho:** Temporary permits are issued only for transfers, not new licenses.
- **Indiana:** There's no interim option for a new store. The state says a permit can't be issued until the whole process is complete, so plan to wait.
- **Ohio:** The state's licensing guide doesn't describe an interim permit for new carryout stores, so plan to wait for the full permit.


Without a temporary permit, don't sell anything until your license is issued. Selling early, including under a previous owner's license after you buy a store, can cost you the application.


## What Delays a Liquor License Application?


Most delays come from a short list of problems, and nearly all of them are avoidable:


- **Incomplete or inconsistent paperwork:** A missing signature, an outdated form, or an ownership detail that doesn't match across documents sends the application back and restarts the clock.
- **Unclear funding or undisclosed owners:** Agencies want to see where every dollar comes from and everyone with a financial interest in the business.
- **Background check issues:** A recent conviction or past license violation by any owner can stall the review or end it.
- **Location problems:** An address that's too close to a school, zoned for a different use, or in a dry area won't get approved, no matter how complete the application is.
- **Protests and hearings:** Objections from neighbors or local officials can add months.
- **Slow local approvals:** Some city councils and licensing boards meet only once a month.
- **Slow responses:** If the agency asks for more information and you take two weeks to reply, your application sits for two weeks. These requests often come with their own deadline, too. In New York, for example, the SLA generally gives applicants about 10 business days to respond, and missing that window can stall the application or end it.


## How to Get Your Liquor License Faster


You can't control the agency's backlog, but you can control almost everything else:


- **Start early.** Give yourself at least six months before your target opening date, and more in quota states.
- **Check the location before you sign a lease.** Confirm zoning, distance rules, and local approval requirements first.
- **Submit a complete application the first time.** Use the agency's checklist, and make sure every owner's details match across every form.
- **Answer agency requests the same week.** Treat them like deadlines to preventcan add weeks or even get the application closed.
- **Get help for complicated cases.** A licensing attorney or consultant is worth the cost if you're buying a license in a quota state, your ownership structure is complex, or your location is likely to draw a protest.
- **Track your status.** Many states, including Texas and Connecticut, let you check your application online.


## When Should You Start the Liquor License Process?


The license is the one step you can't rush, so build the rest of your plan around it. Most of the work of opening a store can happen while your application is under review.


Here's a countdown that keeps both moving at once:


Months before opening Licensing Everything else


6+ Choose your license type, check zoning and distance rules, confirm local requirements Find a location, finalize your budget and financing


5 Form your business, get your EIN and sales tax permit, register with the TTB Sign your lease once the location checks out


4 Get local approval and file your state application Plan your layout, order fixtures and coolers


3 to 2 Answer agency requests, complete any public notice, prepare for inspection Meet distributor reps, set up your POS system, build your online store


1 Follow up on final approval Hire and train staff, plan your opening inventory


0 License in hand Place your first orders and open


Keep a cash cushion for the gap, since rent often starts before you can sell anything. The license is also only one line in your budget, and the full[cost of opening a liquor store](https://www.santehq.com/blog/how-much-does-it-cost-to-open-a-liquor-store) includes inventory, build-out, and several months of operating expenses.


### Know which date you're planning for


"Approved" can mean different things, and mixing them up is where opening budgets go wrong. There are really three dates to track:


- **The day you file:** When the state's clock starts.
- **The day you can legally sell:** Either when your license is issued or, in states that offer one, when a temporary permit is approved.
- **The day the full license is issued:** The official end of the process.


Some states also issue a conditional approval before the final license. It's a good sign, but it doesn't let you sell. Until you hold the license or a valid temporary permit, plan as if the doors are still closed.


### Protect yourself in your lease and purchase agreement


The license timeline should shape your contracts, not the other way around. If you're leasing a space, ask for a licensing contingency that lets you exit or delay rent if the license is denied or runs late, and set a realistic outside date for approval.


If you're buying an existing store, the purchase agreement should name the exact approval that closes the deal, such as the state's transfer approval, and say who covers costs if it takes longer than expected. A licensing attorney can help you draft these terms before you sign.

## FAQ


### How long does it take to get a beer and wine license?


Usually about the same as a full liquor license, or a little less, since the review process is similar. The bigger difference is availability. Beer-and-wine licenses are less likely to be capped by population, so you're less likely to wait for a drawing or have to buy one.


### How long does a liquor license transfer take?


It depends on the state, but expect the state review to take about as long as a new application. Add time for escrow, any required public notice, and local approval.


### How long does federal TTB registration take?


There's no wait. Retailers register with the TTB by filing Form 5630.5d, which is free and can be submitted online. You need to file it before you start selling, and you'll need a separate registration for each location.


### Can you pay to speed up a liquor license application?


Generally, no. Most state agencies review applications in the order they’re received. The fastest way through is a complete application, a location that clearly meets local rules, and quick answers to any follow-up questions.


### How long is a liquor license valid once it's issued?


It depends on the state. California licenses renew every year, while Texas permits run for two years. Missing a renewal can leave you unable to sell, so renewals are a key part of[liquor store compliance](https://www.santehq.com/blog/liquor-store-compliance-guide) .


### What happens if your application is denied?


The agency will usually explain why, and you may be able to request a hearing or reapply once the problem is fixed. In California, for example, a contested application goes before an administrative law judge, who usually issues a proposed decision within 30 days of the hearing for the ABC director to review.


What you can do depends on why you were denied. Paperwork problems or unclear funding can often be fixed and resubmitted, while a location that's too close to a school or sits in a dry area may mean finding a new address. In Massachusetts, if the town turns down a new license, you can't appeal to the state commission and would have to go to court instead.


### Do I need a lawyer to get a liquor license?


No, many owners file on their own. See the cases above where a licensing attorney is worth it.
